newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine pension funds seen key for capital mkts.
newsitem.headline: Argentine pension funds seen key for capital mkts.

text.p: Argentina's private pension funds will be decisive in the development of the local capital markets in the years to come, a top official said.

"Their (the funds) participation as institutional investors within the system is crucial for the expansion of the capital markets and tends to reduce volatility," Jose Luis Pardo, president of the Chamber of Argentine Private Pension Funds, told Reuters. Speaking on the eve of the first convention organized by the Argentine private pension funds system, he forecast the system's rapid expansion.
By 2000 he expects the funds to manage $20 billion against $4.2 billion now. Looking further ahead to 2010, he anticipates close to $100 billion managed by the funds.

"The new pension system, its dynamic, its competitiveness, the development of its services and ability to accumulate savings is provoking a strong impact on Argentina's reality," says the pamphlet introducing the 'Private Pensions, Social Certainty and Economic Growth,' convention.
The funds hold out great hope for the continued reform of Argentina's economy.
Neighboring Chile's private pension system created more than 10 years ago is often cited as one of Latin America's biggest economic success stories.
But Pardo cautions that Argentina's system still has "a long way to go before becoming a net exporter of capital" like Chile's has become.

In addition, Pardo said the recent strong performance of the private pension funds must be considered together with the slump and subsequent recovery in Latin American markets induced by the devaluation of the Mexican peso in December 1994.
In the 12 months ending in the middle of this year, Argentine pension funds posted average returns of just over 20 percent.

"The recuperation of the various markets and the gradual reduction of country risk has to offer lower returns, so it is logical that, in the future, the average return of the system will moderate," said Pardo.

Pardo did not say he expected further lifting of the controls governing the way the funds can invest. Now, up to 49 percent of funds can be invested in stocks and recently the minimum amount allowed to be used on one stock was raised to 2.5 percent from 1.5 percent.

Still, "we do not expect that in the future we will be surprised with any important new investment limitations," said Pardo. Some local observers have called for larger participation by the funds in privatized companies.
The private pension funds were established in August 1994 and currently have some 5.0 million members.
President Carlos Menem will deliver the opening speech at the two-day conference that starts on Tuesday.
